sections.h2: Where is Gallatin, Tennessee, and how did it start?
sections.html:
Gallatin is the seat of Sumner County, on the Cumberland River roughly 30 miles northeast of Nashville. Settlers secured the land along Station Camp Creek early, and Captain William Asher built a fortified station there in 1780. The town was established in 1802 and named for Albert Gallatin, the Treasury Secretary under Jefferson and Madison. Andrew Jackson bought one of the first lots after the 1803 survey, and the town incorporated in 1815.

The Union Army took the town in February 1862 because of its railroad and river position, and Union troops occupied it for the rest of the war. A cholera epidemic hit in the summer of 1873. Historic buildings that survive include Cragfont, Rosemont and Trousdale Place, and the city has a central historic district.

Gallatin has grown quickly. The Census Bureau counted 30,278 people in 2010 and 44,431 in 2020, and its July 2025 estimate is 54,590, a 22.8 percent jump from the 2020 base. Land area is 32.17 square miles.

That pace of growth is the background to the new zoning ordinance the city adopted in 2026, covered below, and to the Station Camp and Liberty Creek school campuses on the list further down.

sections.h2: Which employers keep Gallatin's housing market moving?
sections.html:
Gap, Inc. employs 1,250 workers in Gallatin, and the other large employers named for Gallatin are Sumner Regional Medical Center, now Highpoint Health, Volunteer State Community College and RR Donnelley. The Italian gunmaker Beretta moved its US production to Gallatin in 2015. Meta opened a data center of more than 1.6 million square feet in 2020 and announced a 2024 expansion that would push its Gallatin investment past $1 billion. The Tennessee Valley Authority also runs a coal-fired power plant in the city.

Vol State, part of the Tennessee Board of Regents system, has its main campus in Gallatin and has drawn more than 150,000 students since 1971. Sumner County's unemployment rate was 2.8 percent in March 2025.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about houses in Gallatin?
sections.html:
The median owner-occupied home in Gallatin is worth $372,000 for 2020 to 2024, which is above the national $332,700 and well under Franklin's $705,400. Median monthly owner costs run $1,778 with a mortgage and $552 without. Median gross rent is $1,395, and 57.1 percent of homes are owner-occupied across 19,755 households.

Median household income is $77,518, and 13.0 percent of residents live in poverty. About 33.5 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree.

sections.h2: Which roads and schools matter to Gallatin buyers?
sections.html:
US 31E, also called Nashville Pike or Gallatin Road, is the main street through town. State Route 386, Vietnam Veterans Boulevard, is a controlled-access road that ends in Gallatin and links to Interstate 65. State Routes 109 and 25 complete the network, and WeGo Public Transit runs a daily bus to downtown Nashville. Sumner County Regional Airport has a 5,000-foot runway.

Public schools are run by the Sumner County Board of Education. The Gallatin area includes these campuses:

  • High schools: Gallatin High, Station Camp High and Liberty Creek High
  • Middle schools: Joe Shafer, Liberty Creek, Station Camp and Rucker-Stewart
  • Elementary schools: Benny Bills, Guild, Howard, Liberty Creek, Station Camp, Union STEM and Vena Stuart

Old Hickory Lake and six city parks add recreation, including Lock 4, Triple Creek and Thompson parks.

sections.h2: How are Gallatin property taxes set and paid?
sections.html:
The City of Gallatin sets its rate at $0.5295 per $100 of assessed value for 2026. Sumner County's assessor values the property, and the city says taxes are due by the last day of February, with interest starting March 1. A missing notice does not excuse payment, since Tennessee law does not require mailing one. Payment plans can be arranged through the Recorder's Office.

The city offers relief for qualifying elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners and disabled veteran or widow homeowners, and a tax freeze program that must be recertified every year through the Sumner County Trustee.

Sumner County reappraises every five years. The last reappraisal was 2024 and the next is scheduled for 2029. An owner who disagrees with a value starts with an informal review at the assessor's office, then can appeal to the Sumner County Board of Equalization, which begins meeting June 1. A further appeal to the State Board must be filed by August 1 or within 45 days of the local board's notice, whichever is later.

sections.h2: What do permits and the new zoning rules mean for a Gallatin seller?
sections.html:
Gallatin adopted a new zoning ordinance and zoning map effective September 1, 2026, so older notes on a lot's zoning may be out of date. The Planning Department also handles fences, signs, temporary use permits and flood zone questions. Its commission and zoning appeals board work on a six-week review cycle.

Building permits are applied for through the city's Citizens Self-Service Portal. Contractors must email permits@gallatintn.gov a copy of their state license, general liability and workers' compensation insurance or a state exemption, and a signed city permit bond with a power of attorney before they can apply.

If a past owner finished a basement or added a room, ask the city permit office at permits@gallatintn.gov whether permits were closed. A buyer's lender and inspector will ask the same question.

sections.h2: How is a Gallatin deed recorded?
sections.html:
Deeds for Gallatin houses go to the Sumner County Register of Deeds on North Belvedere Drive. The office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays and records more than 30,000 documents in a typical year. It accepts electronic filing through Simplifile and CSC, and it offers a free MyLandAlert notice that emails an owner when a document is recorded under their name.

The register collects the state conveyance tax, which the Department of Revenue sets at $0.37 per $100 of the purchase price and charges to the grantee. Records are certified back to September 1989 and can be searched online, and deed books and indexes have been digitized back to 1786.

A Gallatin owner who inherited a house or needs to sell on a short timeline should confirm with a title company that the chain of recorded deeds is complete before setting a closing date.

faqs.q: How many people live in Gallatin, Tennessee?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimated 54,590 residents in July 2025, up from 44,431 in the 2020 census. That is growth of 22.8 percent over the 2020 estimates base.

faqs.q: What is the City of Gallatin property tax rate?
faqs.a: The 2026 rate is $0.5295 per $100 of assessed value. Taxes are due by the last day of February, and interest begins March 1.

faqs.q: When did Gallatin's new zoning ordinance take effect?
faqs.a: The city adopted a new zoning ordinance and zoning map as of September 1, 2026. Call the Planning Department at 615-451-5796 to confirm how a specific lot is zoned.

faqs.q: How do I dispute my Sumner County property value?
faqs.a: Ask the assessor, at 615-452-2412, for an informal review first. If that does not settle it, appeal to the Sumner County Board of Equalization, which begins meeting June 1.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed for a Gallatin house?
faqs.a: At the Sumner County Register of Deeds, 355 N. Belvedere Dr., Suite 201, Gallatin. The phone number is 615-452-3892, and electronic recording is available through approved vendors.
